title: Group vertices that can reach each other
description:
In a directed graph, two vertices belong to the same strongly connected component when each can reach the other by following edges forward. Every vertex belongs to exactly one component, so the components split the graph into separate groups.

Implement a function called StronglyConnected that receives the number of vertices and an adjacency list, and returns the graph's components as a list of groups. Vertices are numbered from zero. The adjacency list gives, for each vertex, the vertices its outgoing edges point to.

The answer has to be in one fixed order. Each group lists its vertices in ascending order, and the groups are ordered by their smallest vertex.

StronglyConnected(6, [[1], [2], [0, 3], [4], [3, 5], []]) -> [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]. Here 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 0 is a loop, and so is 3 -> 4 -> 3, so each loop forms one group. The edge 2 -> 3 does not join the two groups, because nothing leads from 3 back to 2. Vertex 5 has no way back to anything, so it forms a group on its own.

Edges going one way only never join vertices: StronglyConnected(3, [[1], [2], []]) -> [[0], [1], [2]].

The hidden tests also check: an edge from a vertex to itself, which still leaves that vertex in a group of one; a graph with no edges; a graph where every vertex can reach every other; a graph in separate pieces, so every piece has to be examined, not just the one the first vertex is in; and an edge pointing into a group that was already completely found earlier, which must not pull the current vertex into that group.

This card asks for the fastest solution, and the tests enforce it: one of them is a graph of over a hundred thousand vertices with a two-second limit. Checking which vertices each vertex can reach gives the right answer but is far too slow. The whole graph has to be sorted into groups in a single traversal that visits each vertex and each edge once.
objective: Recall Tarjan's algorithm: give each vertex a discovery time and a low value, and keep visited vertices on a stack with an on-stack check. Lower the low value from a child's low value after visiting the child, and from a vertex's discovery time when an edge leads to a vertex still on the stack. When a vertex's low value equals its discovery time, pop the stack down to that vertex to get one complete component.

metadata.source: Tarjan's Algorithm to find Strongly Connected Components, GeeksforGeeks (https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/tarjan-algorithm-find-strongly-connected-components/)
